program.name: IAPS
program.organization: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS)
program.roundStatusEvidence: Applications for the Spring 2027 program are now open. Submit your application by September 27, 2026.
program.programDates: Feb 22 – May 14, 2027 (in-person D.C. kickoff Feb 22 – Mar 5, 2027)
program.locationNotes: Fellows choose the D.C. or London track (in person) or Remote. All fellows must attend the two-week in-person kickoff in D.C. (Feb 22 – Mar 5, 2027); IAPS covers travel and accommodation for it but only provides invitation letters for visitor visas. IAPS cannot provide work visas for the U.S. or UK. Remote fellows are possible in "many countries (though we have some exceptions)". The London office has less active programming than D.C.
program.compensation: Stipend of $18,000 (Fellows) or $24,000 (Senior Fellows) for the three-month full-time program, plus $3,000 for the D.C. or London track. Also healthcare benefits, a $500 professional development stipend, and travel and accommodation for the D.C. kickoff. Part-time fellows get a pro-rated stipend.
program.commitment: Full-time (40h/week), about 12 weeks (Feb 22 – May 14, 2027). Part-time options are available for exceptional candidates. Extensions of 4-12 weeks are possible during the fellowship.
eligibilityNotes: D.C. track: only candidates with the right to work in the U.S. between February 22 and May 14, 2027 (no visa sponsorship).
London track: IAPS cannot provide UK work visas. The form asks about the right to live and work in the UK.
Remote track: IAPS can legally hire in many countries with some exceptions. The form asks about the right to work in the chosen country ("Unsure" does not disqualify).
All fellows must attend the in-person D.C. kickoff (Feb 22 – Mar 5, 2027) and get their own visitor visa if needed.
Two roles: Fellow (wide range of career stages) and Senior Fellow (roughly 10+ years of relevant experience, typically including leadership positions; higher stipend).
One application per person: the form blocks an email address that has already submitted.
Applicants must consent to AI processing of their application data (AI-assisted scoring) to complete the form.
Applicants must agree to complete the scored sections without AI, search engines or outside help.
No technical background or policy experience is required (FAQ).

publishedTimeEstimate.text: “The application takes about 45 minutes, in five sections”: About you (5 min), Your experience (5 min), Your motivation (10 min), Communicating with stakeholders (10 min), Timed reasoning (15 min).

aiPolicy.summary: The About-you and Experience sections have no AI rule. Before the Motivation section, applicants must agree not to use AI tools, search engines, outside websites or help from others for the remaining scored sections (Motivation, Communicating with stakeholders, Timed reasoning). IAPS says it can detect this use; the timed section warns that detected use may lead to disqualification.
aiPolicy.quote: Some sections must be completed without AI tools, search engines, or help from anyone else. We will tell you when those sections begin and ask you to agree.

stages.name: Welcome and AI-processing consent
stages.description: Welcome page with a 45-minute estimate and an overview of the sections, then a required consent to AI processing of application data (AI-assisted scoring by Spark Wave on IAPS's behalf).

stages.name: About you (5 min)
stages.description: Basic details and eligibility: names, email, LinkedIn, availability, role (Fellow/Senior Fellow), education, previous applications, location track(s), residence, work authorization per track, D.C. kickoff attendance, optional demographics, referral source, Research/Applied track, Embedded/Independent project.

stages.name: Your experience (5 min)
stages.description: Professional background categories with years and a short description for each, total years of paid experience, 2-3 most important experiences, six knowledge self-ratings, and familiarity with 12 AI-policy concepts.

stages.name: AI agreement
stages.description: Applicants must agree to complete the remaining scored sections without AI tools, search engines, outside websites or help from another person. Declining blocks the application.

stages.name: Your motivation (10 min)
stages.description: Rank 15 AI policy issues by motivation. Write a research interest (200-300 words; Applied-track variant 150-250) and long-term career goals (150-200 words). No AI allowed.

stages.name: Communicating with stakeholders (10 min)
stages.description: One written reply (100-200 words) to a claim made in a meeting with a Congressional office, written as if speaking directly to the person. No AI allowed.

stages.name: Timed reasoning (15 min)
stages.description: Five timed parts, each question with its own countdown and no going back. No AI, search, or outside help.

stages.name: Final questions
stages.description: Optional feedback, consent to share information with other AI-policy organizations, and (for D.C./U.S. applicants) a policy-environment preference. Then Submit and finish.

stages.name: CV upload
stages.description: After submission, the applicant uploads a CV through a linked Airtable form. The confirmation screen calls this "the final step of this application".

stages.name: Work test (mid-October 2026)
stages.description: Shortlisted candidates get two weeks to complete a written task and a short, recorded interview. IAPS will respond to all applicants by October 15. Prompts are not published.

stages.name: Final interview (early to mid-November 2026)
stages.description: Finalists join a live interview with IAPS staff. Final decisions are expected in early December 2026, then supervisor/project matching from Jan 4 to Feb 19, 2027.

program.notes: Prompts marked exact were read from the program definition the live form loads (bold markers removed, links reduced to their labels, and date placeholders filled with the dates the form shows). The welcome page describes the research interest as “up to 300 words” while the question itself says 200–300. Free-text answers are scored with AI assistance, as disclosed in the consent statement. The deadline time and timezone are not stated; it is recorded as end of day US Eastern because IAPS is based in Washington, D.C. The FAQ says the next stage is a written task plus a short pre-recorded interview, then a live interview in November, with selection finalized by early December.

questions.prompt: Having read the statement above, please tick here to confirm you consent to the processing of your application data with artificial intelligence (AI) tools.
questions.notes: Single checkbox under an expandable "Consent Statement" (data controller IAPS; platform and AI-assisted scoring operated by Spark Wave; links to Transparency Notice and Applicant Privacy Notice; retention up to 36 months). The form will not continue without it: "Please check the consent box to continue. If you prefer not to consent to AI processing, you cannot complete this application - contact fellowship@iaps.ai with any questions."

questions.prompt: Please rank the AI policy issues below based on how motivated you are to work on them.
questions.helpText: Place the issue you are most motivated to work on at the top. Drag items to reorder them, or use the dropdowns to set each item's position. Note: if you go back to a previous page, your answers on this page may be erased.
options: catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems that are difficult or impossible to control
controllers of advanced AI gaining immense power
AI based threats to privacy or AI surveillance
issues of intellectual property and copyright raised by AI
misinformation and election integrity issues amplified by AI
excessive energy use caused by AI training or deployment
increasing wealth inequality in society due to AI deployment
AI's effect on education, such as accelerating cheating
large-scale risks from geopolitical instability and great power conflict
questions.notes: Intro: "The next two questions are about what motivates you. The following list contains real AI policy concerns - people differ in which ones they feel most driven to work on, and we want to understand your priorities." 15 issues, shown in shuffled order (options listed in source order). Must rank all items.

questions.prompt: What is a specific research project or specific topic you would be excited to work on during the fellowship, if you are accepted? Briefly explain why you are motivated to work on this project, and the primary intended audience. Be sure to make your response concrete and specific. (200-300 words)
questions.helpText: Note: If you are accepted, you will not work on this exact project. Most fellows are embedded with a supervisor and contribute to that supervisor's projects - though you will have opportunities to pitch your own ideas, and we make a strong effort to match your fellowship work to your interests. We ask this question to understand what excites you and how you think about research, not to hold you to a plan.
questions.notes: Asked if the applicant chose the Research track or Both tracks, under the heading "Your research interests". The welcome page describes this as "a research interest (up to 300 words)". The form rejects answers over 400 words and asks the applicant to shorten them. No minimum is enforced in the code. Answers go to an AI-assisted grader (disclosed in the consent statement).

questions.prompt: Applied Track: What is a specific project or topic you would be excited to work on during the fellowship, if you are accepted? Briefly explain why you are motivated to work on this project. Be sure to make your response concrete and specific. (150-250 words)
questions.helpText: Note: If you are accepted to the Applied track, it is possible - though not guaranteed - that you would work on the project you propose here. We also use this question to understand what motivates you and how you approach applied policy work.
questions.notes: Asked instead of the research-interest question if the applicant chose the Applied track only. Preceded by a reminder of what the Applied track is. The form rejects answers over 300 words.
questions.condition: Asked instead of the research-interest question on the Applied track

questions.prompt: What are your long-term career goals? (150-200 words)
questions.helpText: Please be as specific as possible. Expressing uncertainty about your plans is acceptable, and will not be penalized.
questions.notes: The form rejects answers over 300 words and asks the applicant to shorten them.

questions.prompt: During a meeting with a Congressional office, someone says to you: "AI will never be capable of replacing human labor, since humans have unique intelligence and skills that AI models do not." How would you respond? Please answer as if you're talking directly to the person (in the exact words you would say to them).
questions.helpText: Please answer in 100-200 words.
questions.notes: Intro: “This last written question is about how you communicate in a professional policy setting.” The form rejects answers over 250 words.

questions.prompt: The last section is the timed reasoning section, which takes about 15 minutes.
questions.helpText: Each question has its own countdown timer and cannot be paused, so make sure you will not be interrupted. You must complete this in one sitting. Once you answer a question (or its time runs out), you cannot go back to it. Do not press the back button on your browser. Solve every exercise on your own. Do not use AI, a search engine, or any other external help. We check for this, and detected use of external help may result in disqualification.
questions.notes: Five timed parts, each question with its own countdown: basic syllogisms, multi-premise syllogisms, quantitative questions, short-scenario reasoning, and one-word trivia. Must be completed in one sitting. Extra time is available as an accommodation if requested by email to fellowship@iaps.ai before starting.

questions.prompt: Do you have any feedback on this application process? We read everything, and it helps us improve the experience for future applicants.
